title: Compact sections of a quasi-compact etale geometric fibre
statement:
Let $h:V\to T$ be a separated quasi-compact etale morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-proper-morphism, def-weil-finite-type-morphism, def-weil-etale-morphism]. Let $\Omega$ be an algebraically closed field and $\bar t:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T$ a geometric point [def-weil-geometric-point]. Set $V_{\bar t}=V\times_T\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$, with projection $r:V_{\bar t}\to V$ [def-pc-fibre-product], and let $I$ be the set of morphisms $\bar v:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to V$ satisfying $h\bar v=\bar t$ [def-weil-pbc-geometric-fibre]. Then $I$ is finite and the canonical morphism $\coprod_{\bar v\in I}\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to V_{\bar t}$ is an isomorphism over $\Omega$.

Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $F$ a constant-$A$ module sheaf on $V_{\mathrm{et}}$ [def-weil-pbc-etale-sheaves], and $G=r^{-1}F$ [def-weil-pbc-inverse-image]. Write $H^0_c(V_{\bar t},G)$ for the $A$-module of global sections of $G$ whose closed support of nonzero geometric germs, with its reduced induced closed subscheme structure, is proper over $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ [lem-cbc-proper-support-sheaf-composition, lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme]. Every global section of $G$ has such support, and restriction to the components followed by the inverse-image germ identification gives a natural $A$-linear isomorphism
$$H^0_c(V_{\bar t},r^{-1}F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\bigoplus_{\bar v\in I}F_{\bar v},$$
where stalks are geometric stalks [def-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks]. More precisely, let $W\to T$ be etale, $\bar w:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to W$ lie over $\bar t$, let $t:W\to V$ be a lift over $T$, and let $z\in F(W\xrightarrow{t}V)$. Extend $z$ by zero off the clopen graph of $t$ in $V\times_TW$. The pullback of this section to $V_{\bar t}$ maps to the germ of $z$ at $\bar w$ in the summand indexed by $t\bar w$, and to zero in every other summand.

proof.text: Put $C=V_{\bar t}$ and $q:C\to\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$. Base change preserves etaleness by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-base-change-finite-limits], separatedness by [lem-weil-pbc-separated-base-change], and quasi-compactness by [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-morphism-permanence](3). Thus $q$ has all three properties. Since its base is affine, quasi-compactness means that $C$ is quasi-compact. The base $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ is integral and normal with separably closed function field: its sole local ring and its fraction field are the field $\Omega$, which is integrally closed and algebraically closed.

Apply [sbc-lem-etale-over-normal](1) to $q$. Every nonempty open subscheme of $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ is the whole scheme, so $C$ is a disjoint union of copies $C_j\cong\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ over $\Omega$. The component opens cover $C$; quasi-compactness gives a finite subcover, and disjointness implies that these are all the nonempty components. Each $\Omega$-morphism $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to C$ lands in exactly one component and is the inverse of that component's structure isomorphism, since an $\Omega$-endomorphism of $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ is the identity. By the fibre-product universal property [def-pc-fibre-product], these morphisms correspond exactly to $I$. Consequently $I$ is finite, and the coproduct of these particular maps, indexed by $I$, is the asserted canonical isomorphism. This also covers $C=\varnothing$, when $I=\varnothing$.

Write $\iota_{\bar v}:C_{\bar v}\hookrightarrow C$ for these components. By [lem-weil-pbc-etale-sheaf-clopen-product], restriction identifies $G(C)$ with $\prod_{\bar v\in I}(\iota_{\bar v}^{-1}G)(C_{\bar v})$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-geometric-point-cohomology] to each $C_{\bar v}\cong\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$: its statement identifies component sections with their geometric germs, including at the identity geometric point. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-inverse-image-stalk-germ] first to $\iota_{\bar v}$ and then to $r$. The composite is the canonical isomorphism $\Phi:G(C)\xrightarrow{\sim}\prod_{\bar v\in I}F_{\bar v}$, whose $\bar v$-coordinate is the germ of the section at the component point, identified with $F_{\bar v}$. These identifications are natural in the underlying abelian sheaf. They are $A$-linear: naturality for the endomorphism given by multiplication by each $a\in A$, together with additivity of restriction and germs, proves scalar compatibility.

proof.text: For $s\in G(C)$, the support is exactly the union of those components where the corresponding coordinate of $\Phi(s)$ is nonzero. Indeed each component has one underlying point, and [lem-weil-pbc-geometric-point-cohomology] identifies its section with its germ at every geometric point above that point. In particular the support is a finite union of closed components. Each component with its reduced structure is $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ itself: it is already reduced, so uniqueness in [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme] identifies its structure with the reduced induced one. Its structure morphism is the identity and is proper directly from [def-weil-proper-morphism] (identity diagonal, finite type, and all base changes identity). The ambient $C$ is locally of finite type over $\Omega$, since it is locally the identity by step 2. Therefore [lem-weil-pbc-closed-subset-proper-over-base-union-preimage](1) makes the finite union proper with precisely the reduced-support convention in that node. For empty support the empty morphism is proper directly by the same definition. Thus every section has proper support and $H^0_c(C,G)=G(C)$.

For a finite set $I$, every tuple in $\prod_{\bar v\in I}F_{\bar v}$ has finite support. The inverse of the usual inclusion of the direct sum into the product is explicitly $(m_{\bar v})\mapsto\sum_{\bar v\in I}\operatorname{in}_{\bar v}(m_{\bar v})$. The composites are identity by evaluating each coordinate. Compose this $A$-linear identification with $\Phi$ and the equality in step 4. This gives the claimed isomorphism $H^0_c(C,r^{-1}F)\cong\bigoplus_{\bar v\in I}F_{\bar v}$, natural in $F$ since both maps send a morphism of sheaves to its coordinate stalk maps. The product and direct sum over the empty set are both the zero module.

proof.text: For the generator clause put $P=V\times_TW$, with projections $p:P\to V$ and $\pi:P\to W$. The morphism $\pi$ is separated and etale by the same two base-change lemmas as in step 1; $p$ is etale by base change of $W\to T$. The graph $\gamma=(t,\mathrm{id}_W):W\to P$ is a section of $\pi$. By [lem-weil-pbc-etale-section-clopen-immersion] it identifies $W$ with an open and closed subscheme $D$ of $P$. Apply the clopen sheaf decomposition [lem-weil-pbc-etale-sheaf-clopen-product] to $P=D\amalg(P\setminus D)$ and the sheaf restricted from $F$. The pair consisting of $z$ on $D\cong W$ and zero on its complement glues uniquely to the specified extension section $\widetilde z\in F(P\xrightarrow{p}V)$. Equivalently this is the sheaf gluing axiom for these two disjoint open objects over $V$, so its restriction along $\gamma$ is exactly $z$.

proof.text: The map pulling this section to $C$ is $a=(r,\bar wq):C\to P$. At the $\bar v$-component its pointed image is $(\bar v,\bar w):\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to P$. It lies in $D$ exactly when $\bar v=t\bar w$: a point of the graph with second coordinate $\bar w$ must be $\gamma\bar w=(t\bar w,\bar w)$. Otherwise it lies in the complementary clopen subscheme and the germ of $\widetilde z$ there is zero. In the first case, restriction along the morphism of pointed neighbourhoods $\gamma:(W,\bar w)\to(P,(t\bar w,\bar w))$ identifies its germ with that of $z$, by the colimit definition [def-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks]. Finally [lem-weil-pbc-inverse-image-stalk-germ], applied to $r$ and the pointed etale neighbourhood $(P,(\bar v,\bar w))$ of $\bar v$ on $V$, identifies the germ of the pulled section with this very germ of $\widetilde z$. Thus the coordinate formula for $\Phi$ is the germ of $z$ in the $t\bar w$ summand and zero in every other summand, as required.
